title: Chapter 18: What the River Kept
content: The bell is wrong.

It has been wrong since 1988, when the wheel cracked and nobody had the money to fix it, and it rings a quarter tone flat, and this morning it rings a quarter tone flat for Ade Kessler, and half the people in the pews wince at it out of habit.

Wren stands in the vestibule with her hands wrapped in tape. The blisters have gone bad. The tape is grey and the tape is the only clean thing about her, and she is wearing her grandfather's jacket because it is the only black thing she owns, and the sleeves come down over the tape.
Two hundred seats in the Methodist church on Mill Street. Every one of them is full, and there are people standing at the back and along the side aisle and out on the steps in the cold.

The coffin comes up the aisle on six shoulders. Pine, no fittings, a brass plate with his name and two dates on it. The town paid for it. Ruthie put a coffee can on the counter at the diner and the cannery matched what was in the can, and the man from the funeral home in Marietta drove it up himself and did not send a bill.
The Pruitt brothers carry the front left. Curtis Boone has the back right, cast and all, and when Ruthie's nephew tries to take it from him he does not let go.
In the second row, in order, sit the nine.

Frances Hale with her hand on the back of her daughter's neck. Junie in the red boots. Dale Fisk with his hat on his knees. Nell Acker. The two teenagers, who are sixteen and seventeen and who held hands in the boat and are holding hands now. The Pruitts are up front with the coffin, so their seats are empty until the coffin is set down.
Nobody has said the number out loud in this church. It is in the room anyway, the way cold is in a room.

Reverend Poole is sixty and has buried four people this year and is not good at it. He reads from the twenty-third psalm and then from the obituary the family would have written if there had been a family, and the obituary says Ade Kessler was a deckhand on the Aubrey ferry for nine years and a good man with a boat, and it does not say anything about the water.

At the back, by the door, a man in a Cleveland jacket stands with his hat in his hands. He is twenty-seven and he has his brother's shoulders. He does not come up the aisle. When the pallbearers lift the coffin to carry it out, he is already gone.
"Does anybody wish to speak," Reverend Poole says.
Ruthie stands up in the third row with her purse on her arm like she is about to leave.

"He ate here every Tuesday," she says. "Two eggs, dry toast, coffee. He left a dollar on a two-dollar breakfast for nine years and he never once asked for anything, and when the roof leaked in April he was on it before I could get the ladder." She looks at the coffin. "That is all I have got. It is not enough."
She sits down.
Reverend Poole looks at Wren. Everybody looks at Wren.
She stands up. Her knees are steady, which is strange, and her hands are not, and she puts them behind her back.
"Frances Hale," she says. "Junie Hale. Emmett Pruitt. Ray Pruitt. Dale Fisk. Nell Acker. Curtis Boone. Marla Vance. Peter Vance."
The church is very quiet. The bell is not ringing. Somewhere behind the building a truck idles and somebody shuts a door.
"Ade Kessler," she says. "He went in after a child. The child is alive."
She sits down.
The silence goes on for nine seconds. She counts them, because counting is what she does now, and then Reverend Poole says the benediction and the organ starts and the whole church stands up at once.

The cemetery is on the hill behind the church, and the ground is soup. It rained for two days and stopped at five on Friday morning and has not rained since, and the clay is still holding the water, and the gravediggers have put boards down so that people can stand.
There are two hundred people on the hill and they are standing in two groups.
One group is at the grave, close enough to touch the coffin. The other group is at the road, forty yards back, and they are not talking, and they are watching.

Wren stands at the head of the grave in her grandfather's jacket with her taped hands behind her back and her face dry. She has not cried since the bank on the twelfth of September. She is not going to start on a hill in front of two hundred people, and she can feel them noticing, the way you feel a change in the wind.
Junie Hale comes forward when it is done, holding the plastic horse. Her mother lets her go and she walks to the edge and drops it in and it lands on the pine with a knock that everybody hears.
Then the shovels.
Cora Falk is standing near the headstone with her arms folded, and she says it to the woman beside her, not quietly.
"Nine in that boat."
Wren hears it. The woman hears it. The grave hears it.
"I know," Wren says.
Cora Falk looks at her for a moment and then looks away, and that is worse than a fight.
Hollis Drane is waiting at the gate with a plastic folder under his arm and his coat buttoned wrong.
"Miss Aubrey."
"Mr. Drane."
He holds out the folder. Inside is a Form 9, already filled in at the top, already numbered, and the number is forty-two.
"The county opened it," he says. "On account of there were witnesses. I did not open it. The county did." He swallows. "You have to sign as the operator."
She takes the form. Section 1 is the deceased. Section 3 is the place. Section 6 is the cause, as certified, and the line is blank.
"I cannot certify it," Hollis says. "I am not a certifier. You know I am not a certifier."
"I know what you are."
She takes his pen off his coat without asking. She writes in section 6, in block letters, the way she writes everything now.
DROWNED.
Hollis looks at it for a long time. The wind moves the corner of the paper.
"I cannot accept that," he says.
"You brought me the paper." She folds it and hands it back. "I only filled it in. Put it in the drawer, Mr. Drane. You know where the drawer is."

He takes it. He puts it in the folder. He goes down the hill with his coat buttoned wrong and does not look back, and she knows exactly which drawer it will go in and exactly how long it will stay there.
The Authority issues its statement at noon.
It is one page, on letterhead, signed by the Office of the Director, and Hollis posts it on the Annex door with four pushpins because that is the procedure for public notices.
Wren reads it standing on the sidewalk with the wind coming up Third Street.
"The death of a deckhand on 22 October occurred during a privately operated crossing and is unrelated to gate operations. The Authority extends its condolences to the family."
Unrelated.
She reads it twice. Then she takes the pushpins out one at a time and folds the page in four and puts it in her jacket, and Hollis comes out of the Annex with his hands up.
"That is posted."
"It is filed," she says.
At the house she opens the crossing log at 22 October and writes the page she has been putting off. Ade Kessler. East. Then, under it, in smaller letters: 6:31 p.m. Nine aboard. Nine landed.
Then she puts the Authority's statement in the book, folded, between the pages, and closes it.
By four o'clock she is at the diner because she has not eaten since Thursday and because Ruthie will not bring food to the house, she will only make you come and sit down and eat it in front of her.
The diner is full. It goes quiet when she comes in, which it has done every day this week, and then it starts again, a little louder than before.
Ruthie puts a plate down without being asked and stands there with the coffee pot.
The ledger is on the end of the counter, open, the way it is always open, because Ruthie has never once pretended it is a secret.
Wren reads the page.
Nine in a fourteen-foot boat for two dollars a head.
She came back with the money in her pocket.
He went in for somebody else's child and she came back in the boat.
She has not shed one tear.
Wren reads them twice. Then she takes the pen out of Ruthie's order book and writes under the last line, in her own hand, small and square.
I had nine in the boat and I brought nine back.
Ruthie looks at it. She does not cross it out. She pours the coffee and puts the pot down and says, "Eat your eggs."
At the far end of the counter a man in a feed store cap says, to nobody, "The Authority says it was unrelated."
"It was," Wren says.
The diner goes quiet again. She keeps her eyes on her plate.
"Unrelated to the gate," she says. "The gate did not put nine people in a boat. I did." She cuts the egg. "The Authority was not in the boat. That is the only thing in that statement that is true."
Nobody answers her. The man in the cap pays and leaves, and the door bangs, and Ruthie writes something in the ledger without asking anybody.
Mars comes in at five with her county coat on and a fax cover sheet in her hand.
"Look at the time."
The sheet says 08:52.
"The funeral was at eleven," Mars says.
"I know what time the funeral was."
"They wrote it before the funeral." Mars puts the sheet on the counter. "They wrote it before he was in the ground."

Wren looks at the sheet for a while. Then she takes it and folds it in four and puts it in her jacket with the other one, and she can feel both of them against her chest, two pieces of paper, and she thinks about how much of her life is now paper.
At dusk she comes out of the diner and the lot is full and there is a truck at the end of it under the light, facing out, engine running.
It is a Ford with a dent in the tailgate and a Cleveland Browns sticker on the back window and Ohio plates.
She has not seen that truck since 2023.
The driver's door opens.
highlight: Ade's funeral, a bell a quarter tone flat, and a truck with Ohio plates Wren has not seen since 2023.
